strengths: The paper introduces a novel and timely problem formulation -- 'token sample complexity' -- which cleanly separates the effect of increasing context length at inference time (with fixed trained weights) from classical sample complexity in training. This is a useful conceptual contribution given the rapid growth of context windows in LLMs.

The technical core is substantial and rigorous: the authors adapt empirical process theory (symmetrization, Dudley's entropy integral, chaining for vector-valued sub-Gaussian processes) to handle the key difficulty that queries, keys, and values are drawn from the same finite token set, inducing nontrivial autocorrelation between the attention operator and the aggregated statistic. This is explicitly and convincingly contrasted with the concurrent work of Boursier & Boyer (2025), which does not face this coupling.

The progression from a naive compact-support bound (exponential in R, Theorem 4.2/naive moment bound) to the refined sub-Gaussian analysis (Theorem 5.3, polynomial dependence on scale, rate n^{-β}) is a genuine and non-trivial technical achievement, with a clear proof strategy (radius truncation and balancing of approximation vs. tail error).

The hardmax/infinite-horizon regime (Proposition 5.5) gives an elegant, exact asymptotic result (rate 1/√ln n) via extreme value theory, including a clean explanation of the cancellation phenomenon for symmetric Gaussian inputs, which sharpens intuition about worst-case slow convergence.

Empirical validation is reasonably thorough: synthetic Gaussian experiments closely match the predicted β = 1/(2(1+Ψ)) scaling across a range of horizons, and real-data experiments with BigBird across multiple languages/domains (English, German, Chinese Wikipedia, CC-News) and across 12 layers consistently show sub-parametric convergence rates that degrade with horizon and anisotropy, qualitatively matching the theory's predicted slowdown mechanism.

The appendix includes a careful sharpness analysis for a simple two-point (Dirac mass) example (Theorem B.11), showing the main bound is not tight in R and R0 in that special case, and providing a polynomial-rate alternative -- demonstrating honest engagement with bound quality rather than merely stating unverified claims.
weaknesses: Theorem 5.3 (the paper's main practical contribution) still yields a bound with substantial constants and a restrictive sample-size threshold (n ≥ 4(1/δ-1)n^{1/8}), and does not provide an explicit closed-form dependence of β on A and Σ for real (unknown) token distributions; the connection to the real-data BigBird experiments is therefore largely qualitative/post-hoc, relying on the general intuition of the sub-Gaussian mechanism rather than a directly verified fit of the theoretical formula.

Tightness of the general sub-Gaussian bound is explicitly left open (as stated in the conclusion); only very special cases (two Dirac masses, hardmax Gaussian limit) have matching lower bounds, so it remains unclear how close the established upper bounds are to the true rate in most realistic settings, including the Gaussian case used in Section 6.1 experiments.

The theoretical results assume i.i.d. token sampling, which is a strong idealization for real text (tokens in a sequence are highly dependent and structurally correlated); while the authors acknowledge this and note empirical agreement, no theoretical or empirical stress-test of this assumption's impact is provided beyond the observed power-law fits.

The analysis is restricted to a single self-attention layer; real transformers stack many layers with residual connections, layer normalization, and feedforward blocks, so it is unclear how the derived rates compound or interact across depth, limiting the direct applicability of the theory to end-to-end model behavior (though the paper is transparent about this scope).

The real-text experiments rely on position interpolation to extend BigBird's context to ~500K tokens to build the reference distribution ν, which introduces potential distributional shift/artifacts from extrapolating positional embeddings beyond their trained range; this is not discussed as a possible confound on the reported convergence rates.

The concurrent, independent work of Boursier & Boyer (2025) covers closely related territory (measure-based token sample complexity), which somewhat tempers the claim of novelty, even though the paper articulates real technical differences (dependent tokens, moment convergence vs. Jacobian concentration, smaller β, hardmax asymptotics).

The presentation is very dense with heavy notation and many interleaved definitions/propositions, which, combined with the large number of constants (C, C', q, P, etc.) in the main bounds, makes it hard for a reader to quickly extract the practically relevant takeaway messages without extensive cross-referencing to the appendix.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated theoretical framework ('token sample complexity') that quantifies how quickly finite-context attention approaches its infinite-token (mean-field) limit, addressing a timely question given the push toward very long context windows.

Rigorous mathematical development: uniform convergence of the attention map for sub-Gaussian tokens via a careful adaptation of Dudley's entropy integral/chaining to the vector-valued, ratio-of-empirical-averages structure of softmax attention (handling the non-uniform-Lipschitz kernel and near-zero denominator issues).

The 'attention horizon' H = ||Σ^{1/2}AΣ^{1/2}||_2 is an elegant, interpretable quantity that cleanly unifies the effects of token anisotropy and attention parameters on convergence speed, and is empirically validated as the key driver of the slowdown.

Sharpens the naive O(C(R)/√n) bound (exponential in R, hence practically useless) into a sub-parametric O(C'(R)/n^β) rate with polynomial dependence on scale, via a nontrivial bias-variance/truncation argument (Theorem 5.3), plus an exact asymptotic analysis of the hardmax limit (1/√ln n) with an interesting cancellation phenomenon.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: synthetic Gaussian/sub-Gaussian experiments confirming tightness of theoretical exponents, real-data experiments on BigBird and BERT across multiple languages/domains (7 datasets), and an end-to-end downstream classification task tying the theory to practical accuracy/agreement metrics — with quantitative insight (e.g., 25% of keys recovering most dense-model accuracy).

Thoughtful additional results: sharp two-Dirac-mass example showing where the general bound is loose, a heavy-tailed counterexample showing sub-Gaussianity is necessary, an explicit discussion/experiment on the i.i.d. assumption via windowed sampling, and an appendix (E) improving the exponential-in-R dependence to polynomial under additional regularity.
Clear positioning relative to concurrent work (Boursier & Boyer, 2025), with explicit technical differences (same-token queries/keys/values dependency requiring chaining) highlighted.
weaknesses: The core theoretical setup assumes i.i.d. resampling of tokens from a fixed empirical/population distribution to model 'increasing context length'; this is a stylized proxy that does not directly capture how a real token sequence grows (tokens are ordered, dependent, and often not exchangeable). The windowed-sampling experiment partially mitigates this concern but does not extend the theory itself.

The single-attention-layer, no-positional-encoding, non-causal model is a simplification relative to real Transformers (though multi-head is covered and empirical validation uses full models); the gap between the idealized theoretical object and the actual layer being measured in BigBird/BERT is not fully bridged theoretically.

Constants and rates in the main theorems (e.g., Theorem 4.2, 5.3) are complex and, outside special cases (Gaussian, two-Dirac-mass), their tightness is not established; the paper acknowledges tightness of the general upper bound 'remains widely open.'

The downstream sparsification experiment uses i.i.d. random key subsampling as a stand-in for sparse attention, which is a considerable simplification relative to practical structured sparse-attention mechanisms (Longformer, BigBird's actual pattern, Linformer), somewhat limiting the direct practical takeaway despite the added windowed-sampling check.

Empirical convergence rates are estimated via log–log linear fits over a finite n-range per configuration; robustness/sensitivity of the fitted β to the choice of n-range and to departures from sub-Gaussianity in real text embeddings is not deeply analyzed.

The practical inference-time insight (diminishing returns after ~25% of keys) is qualitatively consistent with existing folk knowledge in the sparse-attention literature, so the incremental practical novelty is moderate even though the theoretical explanation is new.
The dense mathematical presentation (many nested lemmas/propositions in main text and ~40 pages of appendix) may reduce accessibility for a broader ICML audience despite the topic's relevance.
